body.zh-HK:
> 面試官問：一個 draft-assistant 接近 capacity 上限。你有三個選項：調大 dynamic batch、把某個 model path 量化，或在繁忙時 route 到較小的 baseline model。你會如何決定，也如何證明沒有把成本省在最重要的 case 上？
>
> 答啱一半嘅答案：先把 batch 調到最大，再用最低 bit quantisation；如果 output 差一點，才加 fallback。

這個答案有三個常見手掣，但把它們當成一條直線。**Batching** 令多條 request 一齊做可提升吞吐，卻可能令早到的 request 等候湊批；**quantisation** 用較少 bits 表示 weights 或某些計算，可能省 memory 和提高可服務並發，卻可能令某些語言、格式、工具選擇或邊界 case 退步；**fallback** 則不是錯誤發生後才想起的補丁，而是預先定義哪類 request 在什麼證據下可以轉去哪條已知安全路徑。它們共享的問題是：誰的 latency、品質、成本與失敗風險被保護？

## 不要把吞吐當成唯一勝利

先為 request class 定義工作承諾。例如一條互動的短草稿要保護 TTFT 和每 token 的流暢；一條夜間 batch summary 可以接受等候，但要完成在 deadline 前；一條需要嚴格 schema 的 request 必須先過格式 acceptance test。只有一個 global batch size，通常等於把不同承諾攪在一起。較大 batch 可能讓 GPU 更飽和，卻令互動 p99 變差；較小 batch 可能較快開始，但令成本或吞吐不足。

量化也要分模型路徑和 quality slice 看。不要只報「平均分跌得不多」。若一個量化候選令常見英文短答仍好，但特定繁體中文、長 context、JSON schema 或引用邊界失敗更多，這是政策要揭露的 trade-off，不是可以藏起的 noise。fallback 應有契約：觸發訊號、可轉的 model／workflow、保留哪些 input、不可做的後果性動作、誰看告警、以及如何回到主路徑。

想像送貨車。裝滿一車再出發，平均每箱車費會低，但急件會在倉庫等到太久；改用較輕的包裝可放更多箱，但易碎品可能受損；安排備用車不代表任何箱壞了才叫車，而是早已知道什麼天氣、重量或目的地應該換車。好的 policy 是把三個規則放在同一張出車表，不是每遇堵車就隨手扭一個掣。

## 用同一套 fixture 比較候選

建立固定 synthetic workload，刻意包含短互動、長 context、格式嚴格、繁體中文、cache hit/miss 和高峰到達。先跑一條簡單 baseline，例如原 model、保守 batch、明確 queue cap。再每次只替一個 class 改一個選項：batch window、quantised candidate 或 fallback threshold。每次紀錄 queue wait、TTFT、full-response p95/p99、成本 proxy、timeout、fallback rate，以及各 quality slice 的固定 eval result。

把 release gate 寫成否決條件，而不只是「平均要更好」。例如：互動 p99 不可跨過 budget；schema slice 不可低於 baseline；fallback 不可無故變成主路徑；error 或 cancel 上升要能從 trace 解釋。若 quantisation 只替低風險 background class 慳 memory，那可以是合理選擇；若它傷到 critical slice，政策應改為不 route，而不是美化總分。

## 回答容易漏掉的操作面

「用更小 model」仍不是完整 fallback。它可能需要不同 prompt、context cap、output schema、cost cap、review route 或 timeout。batching 又不會修復 upstream retrieval 變慢或 delivery 串流失敗。將三件事放進同一 policy 的原因，是避免成功指標互相騙人：吞吐升了但體驗跌、memory 慳了但格式壞、fallback 維持完成率但默默換成不可接受的答案。

## 可以放進 portfolio 的可檢查 artefact

建立 `serving-policy-matrix`：

- `fixtures/request-classes.jsonl`：虛構工作類別、語言、context、schema 及風險標籤。
- `config/candidates.json`：baseline、batch window、quantised route、fallback trigger 和不可跨越的 guardrail。
- `scripts/replay-policy.mjs`：重播同一組 fixture，寫出 model route、queue、trace 和結果。
- `evidence/candidate-matrix.md`：逐 slice 比較 throughput、tail latency、成本 proxy、quality、fallback rate 和被否決原因。
- `tests/critical-slice-gate.test.ts`：當候選節省成本但 critical slice regression 時 fail。

最有說服力的 demo 不一定是勝出的候選，而是一個被拒絕的候選：它很快、很平，但 policy 顯示它會把不該承受的風險交出去。

## 延伸閱讀

[KV cache 要有 capacity contract](/zh-HK/interview-lab/kv-cache-needs-a-capacity-contract)、[model routing 要有 fallback](/zh-HK/interview-lab/model-routing-needs-a-fallback) 和 [現代 attention、MoE 與 serving 的取捨](/zh-HK/articles/modern-attention-moe-and-serving-tradeoffs)。

## 範圍說明

這是 AI.DOG 的單題練習。model route、quantisation、workload、metric、threshold、artefact 和結果全是虛構 synthetic 本地草稿材料；不歸屬任何公司，亦不代表任何公司現時或過去的面試流程、live system 或 production outcome。

body.en:
> Interviewer asks: A draft assistant is approaching its capacity limit. You can increase dynamic batching, quantise one model path, or route to a smaller baseline model when busy. How would you decide, and how would you prove that savings were not taken from the cases that matter most?
>
> Half-right answer: Maximise the batch first, then use the lowest-bit quantisation. Add a fallback only if the output looks a little worse.

This answer has three familiar controls but treats them as one straight line. **Batching** can improve throughput by processing requests together, but makes an early request wait to form a batch. **Quantisation** represents weights or selected calculations with fewer bits, which can save memory and increase serviceable concurrency, but may degrade particular languages, formats, tool choices, or boundary cases. A **fallback** is not a patch remembered after an error: it is an agreed route for a defined request class when specified evidence says the primary route should not continue. Their shared question is whose latency, quality, cost, and failure risk are protected.

## Do not make throughput the only win

Define a work promise for every request class. A short interactive draft may protect TTFT and smooth output tokens. A nightly batch summary may accept waiting but need to finish before a deadline. A request requiring a strict schema must first pass a format acceptance test. One global batch size often mixes those promises together. A larger batch can fill the GPU more effectively while worsening interactive p99; a smaller batch can start sooner while failing the throughput or cost budget.

Read quantisation by model path and quality slice too. Do not only say that the average score moved little. A quantised candidate may keep common short English answers sound while failing more often on Traditional Chinese, long context, JSON schema, or citation boundaries. That is a trade-off the policy must disclose, not noise to hide. Fallback needs a contract: trigger signal, permitted model or workflow, inputs retained, consequential actions it may not take, alert owner, and a way back to the primary path.

Picture delivery vans. Filling a van before departure lowers average cost per box, but urgent parcels wait too long in the depot. Lighter packing fits more boxes, but fragile goods can be damaged. A spare van is not called only after every box breaks; the dispatcher already knows which weather, weight, or destination merits a different vehicle. A good policy puts all three rules on one dispatch sheet instead of turning a different dial whenever traffic appears.

## Compare candidates with one fixture set

Create a fixed synthetic workload that deliberately includes short interactions, long context, strict formats, Traditional Chinese, cache hits and misses, and peak arrivals. Run a simple baseline first: the original model, conservative batching, and an explicit queue cap. Then change one choice for one class at a time: batch window, quantised candidate, or fallback threshold. Record queue wait, TTFT, full-response p95/p99, a cost proxy, timeout, fallback rate, and fixed evaluation results for each quality slice.

Write release gates as rejection conditions, not only as “the average must improve.” For example: interactive p99 must stay inside its budget; the schema slice cannot fall below baseline; fallback cannot silently become the main path; increases in errors or cancellations must be explained by a trace. Quantising only a low-risk background class may be reasonable. If it damages a critical slice, the policy should stop routing it there rather than beautify the total score.

## The operational layer people often omit

“Use a smaller model” is not yet a complete fallback. It may need a different prompt, context cap, output schema, cost cap, review route, or timeout. Batching does not repair slow upstream retrieval or broken delivery streaming either. Put the three choices in one policy so success metrics cannot fool each other: throughput rises while experience falls, memory is saved while formats break, or fallback keeps completion high by quietly returning unacceptable answers.

## Evidence you could put in a portfolio

Build `serving-policy-matrix` with:

- `fixtures/request-classes.jsonl` containing fictional work classes, language, context, schema, and risk labels.
- `config/candidates.json` specifying a baseline, batch window, quantised route, fallback trigger, and non-negotiable guardrails.
- `scripts/replay-policy.mjs` replaying the same fixtures and writing the model route, queue, trace, and result.
- `evidence/candidate-matrix.md` comparing throughput, tail latency, cost proxy, quality, fallback rate, and rejection reasons by slice.
- `tests/critical-slice-gate.test.ts` that fails when a candidate saves cost but regresses a critical slice.

The most persuasive demo may not be the winner. It may be a rejected candidate that is fast and cheap, while the policy shows it would hand off a risk that should not be accepted.

## Further reading

[A KV cache needs a capacity contract](/en/interview-lab/kv-cache-needs-a-capacity-contract), [model routing needs a fallback](/en/interview-lab/model-routing-needs-a-fallback), and [modern attention, MoE, and serving trade-offs](/en/articles/modern-attention-moe-and-serving-tradeoffs).

## Scope note

This is an AI.DOG standalone practice prompt. The model routes, quantisation choices, workloads, metrics, thresholds, artefacts, and results are fictional synthetic local-draft material. No company is attributed, and this is not evidence of any company’s current or past interview process, a live system, or a production outcome.
